sources.citation: Nesfield, John C. 1883. The Kanjars of Upper India. Calcutta Review 77(154): 368-398.
sources.note: Ethnographic article; says only that 'Kanjars have adopted a secret language of their own, and use the vulgar tongue only when they speak to outsiders' (p. 368). No pronunciation or stress remarks in the scanned range checked.
Lists only Grierson 1922 pp. 95-102 as the descriptive reference (subclassification comment); alternative names Kagari, Kangar Bhat, Kangri, Kanjri. No phonological source.

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (ed.). 1922. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. XI: Gipsy Languages. Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing. Kanjari, pp. 95-102, specimens pp. 103ff., Standard List pp. 180ff.
sources.note: Nothing about stress or accent in the Kanjari section (pp. 95-102: ethnography, sources, districts, noun inflexion, case suffixes, pronouns, verb conjugation, Dravidian element, peculiar words, word-disguising devices) or in the specimens. The only accent remark is the volume-wide transliteration note (scanned line 947): the acute accent is used 'when it is necessary to mark an accented syllable', exemplified with Khowar; no acute accents appear in the Kanjari pages (grep of scanned lines 13270-16400 finds none).

sources.citation: Kirkpatrick, W. 1911. A Vocabulary of the Pasi Boli or Argot of the Kunchbandiya Kanjars. Journal and Proceedings of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, N.S. 7(6): 277-287.
sources.note: Vocabulary with bibliography and ethnographic remarks; only says he tried to catch 'the real phonetic pronunciation' (p. 280). Acute accents in entries (Nimáni 'water', Bá pilo 'father') are Hunterian long-vowel marks, not stress. No stress statement.

No grammar or phonology exists in the bibliography.
Nothing on phonology beyond a paraphrase of Grierson's grammatical remarks; sources cited are Ethnologue, Grierson LSI, Frawley 2003, UNESCO atlas, Mhaiske et al. 2016 (none descriptive).
